doc.areachart_a11y_desc: The wrapper is a figure named from `title`, or from `aria-label` when the chart carries no visible title. The recharts drawing is hidden from assistive technology and the same numbers are exposed as a visually hidden table: one column for `xAxisKey`, then one for each entry in `keys`. Stacked areas are listed as separate columns rather than as the summed height, so a screen reader gets the value of each band, which the filled shape only implies. Series are told apart by colour on screen, so give `keys` names that read well on their own: they become the column headers.

doc.areachart_choice_self_when: When visualizing magnitudes of change over time.
doc.areachart_design_intent: The AreaChart is intended to provide a clear and concise visual summary of complex data patterns.
doc.areachart_i18n_desc: Supports localized number formatting and date strings.

doc.areachart_scenario_2: Bandwidth Usage: Mapping out peaks and troughs in network traffic data.
doc.barchart_a11y_desc: The wrapper is a figure named from `title`, or from `aria-label` when there is no visible title. The recharts drawing is hidden from assistive technology and the values are exposed as a visually hidden table: `xAxisKey` first, then one column per entry in `keys`. Bar length encodes the value against a zero baseline, so here the table and the picture say the same thing; grouping and stacking change the drawing but not the table. The `keys` names are what a screen reader hears in place of the legend.

doc.barchart_anatomy_root: The outermost container managing state and layout.
doc.barchart_best_practice_1: Use BarChart consistently across your application to maintain a predictable user experience.
doc.barchart_best_practice_2: Test BarChart behavior across different screen sizes and input methods to ensure accessibility.
doc.barchart_choice_alt_when: When a simpler alternative like Table better suits the use case.
doc.barchart_choice_self_when: When BarChart functionality with standard options is required.
doc.barchart_design_intent: BarChart provides a consistent, reusable pattern for bar chart visualization for comparing categorical data, reducing implementation effort and ensuring design system compliance.
doc.barChart_long_desc: A chart suitable for comparing and analyzing numerical values across different categories. It is one of the most basic visualizations, allowing for quick grasping of data trends and differences.
doc.barchart_scenario_1: Sales Comparisons: Analyzing monthly revenue across different product departments.
doc.barchart_scenario_2: Inventory Tracking: Displaying stock levels for various item categories in a warehouse.
doc.boxplot_a11y_desc: The drawing is hidden from assistive tech and the same summaries are published as a data table underneath, one row per group with all five numbers. Give the chart a name with title, or with aria-label when the heading lives elsewhere on the page.
doc.boxplot_best_practice_1: Compute the five numbers before passing them in, and be explicit about whether the whiskers exclude outliers — the chart draws what it is given and cannot say which convention produced it.
doc.boxplot_best_practice_2: Watch for groups whose ranges differ by an order of magnitude: on one linear axis the smaller groups flatten into lines, and the table becomes the only way to read them.
doc.boxplot_choice_alt_when: One number per category is the whole story.
doc.boxplot_choice_matrix_desc: Reach for a box plot when the spread is the point, and for a simpler chart when a single number per group is enough.
doc.boxplot_choice_scatter_when: You have the individual observations and want to show every one of them.
doc.boxplot_choice_self_when: You need the spread, the middle, and the extremes of each group side by side.
doc.boxplot_desc: Five-number summary of a distribution per group
doc.boxplot_design_intent: A box plot is read by position within a range, not by length from zero, so the axis is fitted to the data rather than anchored at zero. Groups share one hue: what separates them is the label on the axis, and changing hue per group would suggest they are different kinds of thing rather than the same measurement in different places.
doc.boxplot_long_desc: BoxPlot shows how values are spread within each group — response times per endpoint, salaries per role, scores per class. It draws the five-number summary, so two groups with the same average still look different when their spreads differ.
doc.boxplot_scenario_1: An operations dashboard compares response times per endpoint, showing that a good median hides a long tail.
doc.boxplot_scenario_2: A compensation review puts salary bands per team side by side without exposing individual figures.
doc.candlestickchart_a11y_desc: The drawing is hidden from assistive tech and the same periods are published as a data table underneath, one row per period in open / high / low / close order. Give the chart a name with title, or with aria-label when the heading lives elsewhere on the page.
doc.candlestickchart_best_practice_1: Pass the periods oldest first. The chart draws them in the order it receives them and has no way to tell a reversed series from a rising one.
doc.candlestickchart_best_practice_2: Keep the periods evenly spaced. Skipping empty periods silently compresses time, which makes a quiet stretch look like a sudden move.
doc.candlestickchart_choice_alt_when: One value per point is enough and the shape of the series is the story.
doc.candlestickchart_choice_boxplot_when: You are comparing distributions across groups rather than following one series through time.
doc.candlestickchart_choice_matrix_desc: Reach for candlesticks when each period has four numbers, and for a simpler chart when it has one.
doc.candlestickchart_choice_self_when: Each period has an opening, a closing, and a range, and the relationship between them matters.
doc.candlestickchart_desc: Open, high, low and close per period
doc.candlestickchart_design_intent: Rising and falling periods are separated by shape first — a hollow body for rising, a filled one for falling — and only then by colour, so the series survives greyscale and colour-vision differences. The body is left unpainted rather than filled with a surface colour, because the chart does not paint its own background and would otherwise show as a white block on a tinted page.
doc.candlestickchart_long_desc: CandlestickChart shows how a value opened, ranged, and closed within each period — a price series, a daily temperature range, a load metric per hour. Each mark carries four numbers, so the reader sees how far the value travelled, not only where it ended up.
doc.candlestickchart_scenario_1: A portfolio view shows the week's share price, where a flat close hides a day that moved and came back.
doc.candlestickchart_scenario_2: A weather panel shows each day's temperature range alongside the morning and evening readings.
doc.funnelchart_a11y_desc: The wrapper is a figure named from `title`, or from `aria-label` when there is no visible title. The recharts drawing is hidden from assistive technology and the stages are exposed as a visually hidden table with two columns, `nameKey` and `dataKey`. The tapering shape only implies how much is lost between stages; the table gives the absolute value at each one, so the drop-off can be worked out instead of estimated from the width.

doc.gaugechart_a11y_desc: This chart is deliberately handled differently from the others. The value is already rendered as visible text in the middle of the arc, so no hidden table is added: a second copy of the same number would only be announced twice. What was missing was the name, so the wrapper is a figure named from `title`, or from `aria-label`. The arc holds no text of its own and is not hidden, because hiding it would take the value with it. Pass `label` when the raw number needs a unit or formatting.

Pairs with no data stay empty rather than reporting zero, because an absent measurement and a measured zero are different facts.

doc.sankeychart_a11y_desc: The drawing is hidden from assistive tech and the same flows are published as a data table underneath, one row per flow (from, to, value). Give the chart a name with title, or with aria-label when the heading lives elsewhere on the page — that name becomes the table's caption.
doc.sankeychart_best_practice_1: Keep the flows out of a stage equal to the flows into it, and give the leftover its own node ("Left", "Unspent") — a Sankey that silently loses volume reads as if the loss never happened.
doc.sankeychart_best_practice_2: Stay under roughly a dozen nodes. Past that the bands cross too often to follow, and a table or a grouped bar chart carries the same numbers better.
doc.sankeychart_choice_alt_when: Things are connected but nothing measurable flows along the edges.
doc.sankeychart_choice_funnel_when: One quantity only shrinks through an ordered set of steps, with no branching.
doc.sankeychart_choice_matrix_desc: Reach for a Sankey when the amounts moving between stages are the point, and for a simpler chart when they are not.
doc.sankeychart_choice_self_when: A quantity splits, merges, or leaks between named stages and the sizes matter.
doc.sankeychart_desc: Flow chart where band width is the amount
doc.sankeychart_design_intent: A Sankey is read by thickness, so the chart is honest only when every flow out of a stage is accounted for. Bands take the colour of the stage they leave, which is how the eye follows one source across the whole diagram; node labels are drawn in text colour, not series colour, so a pale stage stays readable.
doc.sankeychart_long_desc: SankeyChart shows how a quantity splits and recombines as it moves through stages — where traffic goes, where a budget ends up, where applicants drop out. The width of each band is the amount flowing through it, so the reader compares volumes by looking rather than by reading numbers.
doc.sankeychart_scenario_1: An acquisition dashboard shows which channels reach the pricing page and how many of them sign up rather than leave.
doc.sankeychart_scenario_2: An operations view traces orders from placed to shipped, with the back-ordered and returned branches drawn to scale.
doc.scatterchart_a11y_desc: The wrapper is a figure named from `title`, or from `aria-label` when there is no visible title. The recharts drawing is hidden from assistive technology and every point is exposed as a visually hidden table: the point name, then `xAxisName` and `yAxisName` as column headers. A fourth column appears when at least one point carries a `z`. A scatter plot is read as a cloud, and clustering and outliers are properties of the picture rather than of any single row, so a summary sentence next to the chart is still worth writing.

doc.sparkline_a11y_desc: Provide an ariaLabel summarizing the trend (e.g. "Revenue up 12% over 7 days"); without one, the sparkline is decorative and hidden from assistive tech, so the adjacent value carries the meaning.
doc.sparkline_best_practice_1: Fix the y-domain with min and max when comparing several sparklines so their heights are comparable.
doc.sparkline_best_practice_2: Use color to signal direction (positive vs. negative) rather than to distinguish many series.
doc.sparkline_choice_alt_when: The reader needs axes, tooltips, or exact values.
doc.sparkline_choice_matrix_desc: Use a Sparkline for compact, inline trends and a full chart when the reader needs to read values.
doc.sparkline_choice_self_when: Show a trend inside a cell, tile, or list row with no need for axes.
doc.sparkline_design_intent: A sparkline trades precision for density: no axes, labels, or gridlines, just the trend line at a glance. It is meant to sit beside a number, not replace a full chart.
doc.sparkline_long_desc: Sparkline is a tiny, axis-free chart for embedding a trend inline — inside a table cell, a Stats tile, or a Leaderboard row — where the shape of the data matters more than its exact values.
doc.sparkline_scenario_1: A DataGrid column shows each row's 30-day trend next to its current metric.
doc.sparkline_scenario_2: A Stats tile pairs a headline number with a sparkline of its recent history.

Nested data is flattened to its leaves because only leaves are painted as tiles, so a grouping level that is never drawn is never listed either. Area encodes the value on screen and area is not announced, which leaves the table carrying the whole comparison.

doc.waterfallchart_a11y_desc: The drawing is hidden from assistive tech and the same steps are published as a data table underneath, one row per step, carrying both the change and the running total after it. Give the chart a name with title, or with aria-label when the heading lives elsewhere on the page.
doc.waterfallchart_best_practice_1: Mark the opening and closing columns with total so they are drawn from the baseline — a closing figure drawn as a floating change reads as one more small adjustment rather than the answer.
doc.waterfallchart_best_practice_2: Keep the steps in the order they actually happen. A waterfall sorted by size stops being arithmetic and becomes a ranking with misleading connective tissue.
doc.waterfallchart_choice_alt_when: You are showing the parts that make up one total, with no order and no arithmetic.
doc.waterfallchart_choice_matrix_desc: Reach for a waterfall when the steps between two totals are the point, and for a simpler chart when they are not.
doc.waterfallchart_choice_sankey_when: Amounts move between stages and can split or merge, rather than accumulating in one running total.
doc.waterfallchart_choice_self_when: A total is built up or worn down by named contributions, and the size of each matters.
doc.waterfallchart_desc: Running total broken into its contributions
doc.waterfallchart_design_intent: Every bar is an amount and a direction, so the chart is only honest when the steps actually add up to the totals it draws. Colour separates added from removed, but the signed value is printed on each bar as well — the direction must survive being read in greyscale, and "increase" is not the same claim as "good".
doc.waterfallchart_long_desc: WaterfallChart shows how a starting number becomes an ending number, one contribution at a time — revenue to profit, last month's headcount to this month's, a budget to what is left of it. Each bar floats between the running total before and after that step, so the arithmetic is visible rather than implied.
doc.waterfallchart_scenario_1: A finance dashboard walks from quarterly revenue down to profit, one cost line at a time.
doc.waterfallchart_scenario_2: An HR view shows opening headcount, hires, leavers, and the closing number, with a mid-year subtotal.
